en: INTRODUCTION (Nidāna) I. Success!

Those who have not gone forth and those who are not ordained [have departed]. The Saṃgha is assembled in its entirety. What is to be done by the Saṃgha? Venerable ones, announce the consent and the purity of those who have not yet arrived. Once it has been announced—
And as he announced: "Venerable ones, one month less one night of the summer season has passed; three months plus one night remain.
Old age and death are approaching; the teaching of the Teacher is falling into ruin."
The life-faculty is impaired;
the True Dharma departs; practice declines; laxity arises;
and the gates to the miserable realms are flung open.
The gates of the deathless are closed; the bridge of Dharma is cut; the ship of Dharma is shattered; the raft of Dharma sinks;
the torch of Dharma is extinguished;

the tree of Dharma is uprooted; the banner of Dharma falls; the banner of Māra is raised high; the ocean of Dharma dries up; Mount Sumeru of wisdom is scattered; and the tigers among speakers go to their setting.
For those who serve as helmsmen and instructors on the true path will soon be perceived by men as mere deer. Therefore, all you venerable ones,

being agitated and filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), [should pay homage] to that Wheel-turning King of Dharma, the possessor of the unsurpassed ten powers, who has arisen from the maturation of his ancient deeds of virtuous conduct.

For one who has abandoned false speech, slander, harsh words, and idle chatter, [the teaching] consisting of speech that conforms to truth—this instruction and admonition should be heard. "Venerable ones, you must apply yourselves with heedfulness; for it is through heedfulness that the awakening of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones was attained, as well as all other wholesome qualities conducive to awakening. It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs (*śāsayati*), and this [teaching] indeed instructs correctly.
The Prātimokṣa is for the sake of liberation; therefore, this scripture is preeminent.
Whatever is to be done or not done by a monk, and whatever is improper or proper to be spoken—all that has been revealed here in its entirety by the Sage in this Prātimokṣa. (1–2)
It restrains one from the threefold misconduct and enjoins one in the threefold virtue;
it increases the side of wholesome qualities and exhausts the faults that are the enemies of virtue;
it destroys ignoble wrong livelihood, which leads to miserable rebirths.
And he gradually purifies the path to heaven and liberation.
As long as this [teaching] revealed by that Lord of the World shall endure,
for so long shall the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas remain in this world.
Therefore, for the sake of your own welfare and for the long-term endurance of the Teaching, listen with focused attention for a moment; I shall recite the Prātimokṣa.
May the venerable Saṅgha listen: today is the fifteenth-day Poṣadha of the Saṅgha. If it is the proper time for the Saṅgha, [let it proceed].

It is agreeable and the Saṃgha consents that the entire Saṃgha should today perform the Poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa-sūtra; this is the motion. "Venerable ones, we shall perform the Poṣadha and we shall recite the Prātimokṣa-sūtra;
therefore, all of you listen well, attend thoroughly, and pay close attention."

Whosoever among you has committed an offense must disclose it; if there is no offense, one should remain silent. By remaining silent, we shall know that the Venerable Ones are pure. And just as there is a formal response for each individual monk when questioned, even so does this proclamation proceed three times before such an assembly of monks.

Furthermore, if a monk, in such an assembly of monks, even when it has been proclaimed up to three times, does not disclose an offense he remembers while being conscious of it, he commits a deliberate lie. And, venerable ones, a deliberate lie has been called by the Blessed One an obstructive factor. Therefore, a monk who has committed an offense and seeks purification [should disclose it].

One who remembers an offense should disclose it; having disclosed it, there is ease for him, but not by failing to disclose it. Venerable ones, I have recited the introduction to the recitation of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra.
In this matter, I ask the Venerable Ones: Are you pure in this? A second time, and a third time, I ask: Are you pure in this?
Since there is silence, the Venerable Ones are pure in this; thus do I understand.
I. The Pārājika Dharmas.
Furthermore, venerable ones, these four pārājika dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Whatever monk, having entered into the training together with the monks, without having renounced the training...
If a monk should engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, without revealing his weakness of faculties, he is defeated (*pārājika*) and no longer in communion.

Furthermore, if a monk should take what is not given, which is reckoned as theft, such that for taking what is not given the king, having seized him, would have him executed, imprisoned, or banished, and should say of him: "You are a thief, you fool! [he is defeated].
If a monk, taking what is not given, should say such things as "You are a fool" or "You are a thief," he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.

Furthermore, if a monk should intentionally deprive a human being of life with his own hand, or provide him with a weapon, or seek out a weapon-bearer for him, or should speak to him thus: "O man, why [do you live]? [he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion.]
If, with the thought "Death is better for you than this wretched,
miserable life," he should, in many ways, incite another to death or praise the merits of death, and that person should die as a result of that means,
then this monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. 3.
Furthermore, if a monk, not knowing and not fully understanding, should claim to have attained a superhuman state, a state of excellence belonging to the noble ones, or knowledge or vision,
saying "I know" or "I see," and if at a later time he, whether being questioned or not being questioned, speaks thus:

If one who does not know says "I know," or one who does not see says "I see"—speaking what is empty and false, except out of overweening pride—this monk also becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. 4.

Venerable sirs, I have recited the four *pārājika* rules, by the transgression of any one of which a monk does not obtain communal residence or communion with the monks; as it was before, so it is after—having fallen into a *pārājika*, he is one who is no longer in communion. In this regard, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter?
A second time and a third time I ask: Are you pure in this matter? Are you pure here, venerable sirs? Since there is silence, it is thus that I understand it.
II. The Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas.
Furthermore, Venerable Ones, these thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
Intentionally emitting semen, except during a dream, is a Saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. 1.

Furthermore, if a monk, with a mind that is excited and perverted, should engage in physical contact with a woman— whether by taking her hand, taking hold of her hair, or touching or stroking any other part of her body— it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Furthermore, if a monk, with a mind that is excited and perverted, should address a woman with lewd, wicked, and vulgar speech associated with sexual intercourse, as a young man would address a young woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Thus ends the third *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rule:

Should any monk, with a mind that is excited and perverted, speak in the presence of a woman in praise of his own personal service, saying, "Sister, this is the foremost of all services," [he commits an offense].
If one should serve a monk like me— one who is virtuous, possessed of wholesome qualities,

and living the holy life— with this practice, namely that which is connected with sexual intercourse, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. Furthermore, if a monk should engage in matchmaking— whether for a woman with the consent of a man, or for a man with the consent of a woman, whether for marriage or as a paramour— even for a single moment— it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

When a monk is having a hut built by his own request—being ownerless and for his own use—he should have it built according to the proper measurements. Herein, the measurement of the hut is twelve spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and seven spans across at the interior. That monk must have other monks brought to inspect the site; the monks who have been brought must inspect the site so that it is free from harm and has sufficient space for movement.

If a monk, while undertaking a building site that is not free of danger, should have a small hut built for himself by his own request, without an owner, and without having led other monks to inspect the site, or should exceed the prescribed measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
(6) When a monk is having a large dwelling built for himself by his own request and with an owner, that monk must lead other monks [to inspect the site].
A site should be designated by monks who have been instructed to designate a site; [the site] must be free from harm and have sufficient space.
If a monk [designates] a site that involves harm...

If a monk, while having a large monastery built for himself with a patron, does not have the monks summoned for the inspection of the site, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. (7) Furthermore, if a monk, being wicked and out of malice, being dissatisfied [with a pure monk], [accuses] a pure monk [of an offense]... [without grounds].

If one should falsely accuse another with a groundless *pārājika* offense, thinking, "In this way I shall cause him to fall from the holy life," and when that person is thoroughly and properly interrogated and examined, that legal case is found to be indeed groundless, yet the accusing monk persists in his fault; [he is guilty].
“I spoke out of malice,” [if he says this regarding a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is] *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
8. Furthermore, if a monk, being malicious and dissatisfied due to malice, regarding some legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that belongs to another category...
If, having grasped even a mere fraction of a matter, one should falsely accuse a monk who is not guilty of a *pārājika* offense with a *pārājika* offense,

thinking, "In this way I shall cause him to fall from the holy life (*brahmacarya*)," and when that case is thoroughly investigated and examined, it is found to be otherwise than what was alleged; [this is a formal act of censure].
If a monk, through some legal dispute, should adopt even a mere fragment of a different position,
and the accuser should persist in his accusation, saying, "I spoke [this] out of malice," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Furthermore, if a monk should strive for the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, or should support a legal dispute conducive to schism...

If that monk persists in taking up and maintaining [the dispute], those monks should say to him: "Venerable one, do not strive for the schism of the harmonious Saṃgha; do not persist in taking up and maintaining a legal issue conducive to schism. Venerable one, let there be unity with the Saṃgha; for the Saṃgha is harmonious, united, living in concord, and free from dispute."

Being of one mind, with a single purpose, and having become like milk and water mixed together, he dwells in comfort and ease. "Venerable one, relinquish this matter that causes a schism in the Saṅgha!

If, even when addressed by the monks in this manner, that monk persists in taking up and adhering to that very matter and does not relinquish it, that monk is to be admonished by the monks up to three times regarding that matter.
If, even after being admonished up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it, he should relinquish that matter, that is well; but if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If there should be monks who follow that monk and speak in discord—whether one, two, or many—
Or they might say to those monks: "Venerable ones, do not say anything at all regarding this matter to the monk named so-and-so.
For what reason? Because this monk speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya, and he speaks in accordance with our own will and inclination."
"This monk speaks knowing [the truth] and not unknowing; and that which is pleasing and acceptable to this monk is also pleasing and acceptable to us.

Those monks should be addressed by the other monks as follows: "This monk does not speak according to the Dharma, nor does he speak according to the Vinaya. Taking up what is contrary to the Dharma and contrary to the Vinaya, he disputes and persists in his assertion.
Release [this position]!"

"But, venerable ones, you are following the schism of the Saṃgha and speaking divisively; for the Saṃgha is indeed united, harmonious, living in mutual joy, without dispute, single-minded, having a single objective, and having become like milk and water mixed together, dwelling in comfort and ease. If, monks, those monks are thus addressed by the monks..."

If those monks, being without shame, should persist in taking up and maintaining that very matter and not relinquish it, those monks are to be admonished by the other monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter. If, being admonished up to three times, they relinquish that matter, that is well; if not, [they are to be dealt with according to the rule].
[If they] should expel [him], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. 11.
Furthermore, if a monk should dwell depending upon a certain village or town, and he should be a corrupter of families and a wicked person...
His conduct may be seen, heard, or known to corrupt families; his evil practices may be seen, heard, or known,
and he may be a defiler of families and one of evil conduct.
That monk should be addressed by the monks in this way: "Venerable one, you are a corrupter of families and a practitioner of evil conduct;
your corruption of those families is seen, heard, and known, and your evil practices are visible."
He is seen, heard, and known even by you; yet this venerable one is a corrupter of families and of evil conduct.
Let this venerable one depart from this residence; enough of your staying here.

If that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, should speak to those monks as follows: "Venerable ones, these monks are swayed by favoritism, swayed by hatred, swayed by fear, and swayed by delusion;

for while they have fallen into such an offense, they expel some monks and do not expel others," then that monk should be addressed by the monks as follows: "These monks are not swayed by favoritism, nor..."

He does not go out of favoritism, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion; rather, it is you, Venerable One, who are a defiler of families and of evil conduct. Your defilement of families is seen, heard, and known;

your evil practices are also seen, heard, and known. Since you, Venerable One, are a defiler of families and of evil conduct, may the Venerable One relinquish this speech that proceeds from favoritism and proceeds from hatred.
If that speech leads to fear and leads to delusion,

and if that monk, being thus addressed by the monks, persists in taking up and clinging to that very matter and does not relinquish it, then that monk should be formally admonished by the monks regarding that matter up to three times.
If, being exhorted up to three times for the sake of relinquishing it, he should relinquish that matter, that is well; but if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Furthermore, in this case, a certain monk might be of a difficult-to-speak-to nature; when being addressed according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya by monks regarding the training rules included in the recitation, he makes himself unaddressable.

"Venerable sirs, do not say anything to me, whether good or bad; I too shall not say anything to the venerable ones, whether good or bad. Venerable sirs, desist from speaking to me; enough of your speaking."

That monk should be addressed by the monks as follows: "Venerable one, when you are being spoken to in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya by the monks regarding the training rules included in the recitation, do not make yourself unaddressable; let the venerable one make himself addressable."

Monks, they shall speak even to him in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya: "Let the Venerable One also speak to the monks in accordance with the Dharma and in accordance with the Vinaya. For thus has the assembly of that Blessed One grown—that is to say, through mutual admonition, mutual instruction, mutual exhortation, and mutual restoration from offenses. Let the Venerable One relinquish [this matter].
If that monk, when being addressed by the monks in this manner, does not [abandon] his state of having an unadmonishable course of action regarding himself...
If that monk, having taken up and grasped that matter, persists in it and does not relinquish it, he should be admonished by the monks up to three times for the sake of relinquishing that matter.
If, being admonished up to three times, he relinquishes that matter, that is well; but if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. 13.
Venerable ones, I have recited the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules: nine that entail immediate offense and four that persist until the third admonition.
If a monk has committed any one of these rules and knowingly conceals it for as long as he does so, for that duration he must undergo *parivāsa* against his will.

A monk who has spent [the period of] *paryuṣita* and *parivāsita* must undergo a further *mānāpya* of six nights within the Saṃgha. Once the *mānāpya* has been performed, that monk—being bound by the *ābṛhaṇa* and having fulfilled the legal requirement (*kṛtānudharma*)—is to be rehabilitated (*ābṛhitavya*) where there is a community of twenty monks. If a community of monks numbering fewer than twenty should rehabilitate that monk, that monk [remains suspended].
And those monks who have not been suspended are to be censured; this is the proper procedure therein. In this matter, I ask the Venerable Ones:
Are you pure in this? A second time, and a third time, I ask: Are you pure in this?
Since there is silence, the Venerable Ones are pure in this; thus do I understand it.
III. These two indeterminate matters, moreover, venerable sirs, come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.

Furthermore, if a monk should sit down in private on a concealed seat with a woman, one-on-one, in a manner conducive to sexual intercourse, and a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy should charge him with one or another of three categories of offenses—
whether a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyantika* offense— and the monk admits to having sat down [with her], [he is guilty].
He is to be dealt with according to one or another of the three categories of offenses— whether it be a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyantika*—
by whichever offense a trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*) may have spoken of that monk, by that very offense is that monk [to be dealt with].
This dharma is to be proclaimed as indeterminate.

One should not arrange a seat in a secluded, concealed place; nor should one sit with a person of the opposite sex who is capable of sexual intercourse, except for [the purpose of] that [instruction].

If one should address a village of women with wicked, sinful, and indecent speech connected with sexual intercourse, and a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy should charge him with either of two offenses— either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyantika* offense—
then the monk, if he admits to having sat [with them], shall be dealt with according to either of those two offenses.

Whether it be for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, or a *pāyantika*, or whatever offense a trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*) may speak of that monk, by that very offense must that monk be dealt with. This rule, too, is indefinite (*aniyata*).
These two have been recited by me, O Venerable One.

There are two indeterminate factors; regarding these, I ask the Venerable Ones: "Are you pure in this matter? A second time, a third time I ask: "Are you pure in this matter? Since there is silence, the Venerable Ones are pure in this regard; thus do I understand it.
IV. The *niḥsargika-pāyantika* rules:
Furthermore, venerable ones, these thirty *niḥsargika-pāyantika* rules come up for recitation every half-month in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.

1. When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, a monk may keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. If he should keep it longer than that, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyantikā).
2. When a robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended, a monk shall not be separated from any one of his three robes for even a single night, except with the consent of the Saṃgha;
[if he does so], it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyantikā).

When a monk whose robe has been finished and for whom the *kaṭhina* has been suspended should obtain an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*), that monk, if he desires it, may accept it. Having accepted it, if it should be completed [in size], he must make it up quickly and keep it;
if it should not be completed, that monk may set that robe aside for a maximum of one month.
If, while there is an expectation of obtaining a robe, one should set aside [money] beyond that amount for the sake of completing what is deficient, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense.
(3) Furthermore, if a monk should have an unrelated nun wash, dye, or beat an old robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense. (4)

5. If a monk should receive a robe from a nun who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyantika*). 6. If a monk should request a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except on a specific occasion, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture once the robe has been completed. In this case, the specific occasion is when a monk’s robes have been stolen or his robes have been lost.
Whether his robes have been burnt or his robes have been carried away— this is the proper occasion.
A monk whose robe has been snatched away, or whose robe has been lost, or whose robe has been burned, or whose robe has been carried off,
may request a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative... (If that monk...)
Kṣuṃ śrāddhaḥ
If a householder or a householder’s wife should offer many robes, that monk, if he so desires, may accept at most an inner robe and an upper robe.
Then he should accept the robe; if he should accept it beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyantikā*.

Furthermore, if a householder or a householder’s wife who is not related to a monk should set aside funds for robe-material, thinking, "With these funds for robe-material, I shall [procure] such a robe..."
Having had such a robe made, thinking, "I shall clothe the monk named so-and-so," if that monk [previously]...

Being invited, he approaches a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative and, having formed some kind of pretext, should say: "Those robe-funds which have been prepared by you, venerable sir, on my account— with these..."
Having had such a robe made by means of such an amount of money,
he...
"Thinking, 'I shall clothe the monk named so-and-so,' [he says: 'It is well, venerable sir; having had such and such robes woven with those robe-funds, clothe me with that robe.'"
"Cover [me]," out of a desire for something beautiful; when the robe has been completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, if two unrelated householders or householders' wives, having set aside individual robe-funds specifically for a monk, were to say: "With these robe-funds, we two..."
"Having had individual robes of such and such a kind prepared, we two shall clothe the monk named so-and-so with these two individual robes.
In that case, if that monk, having not been previously invited, approaches those two unrelated householders...

Or, if the two householders' wives, having fallen into some such deliberation, should say: "Those robe-funds which have been prepared by you, venerable sirs, on my account—with these very robe-funds, having caused a robe of such and such a kind to be made for each of us, we shall clothe the monk named so-and-so; it would be well, venerable sirs, if with those robe-funds [you were to cause] a robe of such and such a kind [to be made for each of us]."
If, having intended to provide each with a separate robe,
two people together provide one robe for me out of a desire for something more excellent, then when the robe is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense. 9.

Furthermore, if robes for a monk have been sent by a king, a royal minister, a brahmin, or a householder, in the hand of a messenger, and that messenger, having approached that monk, should say: "Venerable sir,
these [robes] for you have been sent by a king or a royal minister..."
Or by this [means], whether by a Brahmin or by a non-Brahmin.
"If a householder has sent robe-funds, let the Venerable One accept these robe-funds out of compassion.
That monk should say to that messenger: "Venerable messenger, it is not permissible for monks to accept robe-funds."
"Having received a robe that is timely and permissible, we accept it with our own hands and, having quickly made it up, we wear it.
That messenger should say to that monk: "Is there anyone among the venerable ones who acts as a steward (vaiyyāpatyakara) who performs services for the monks?"
A monk who requires robes should designate a steward, whether a monastery attendant or a lay follower, saying: "This person performs services for the monks.

That messenger, having approached that steward, should speak thus: "Venerable steward, these robe-funds have been sent by a king, or a royal minister, or a brahmin, or a householder, for [the monk] named so-and-so."
"Sent for the sake of a monk: 'It would be well, venerable steward, if you were to purchase such and such a robe with these robe-funds;
that monk will come to you at the proper time, and you should clothe him with a robe that is allowable.'"
Having thus properly and thoroughly instructed that attendant, the messenger should approach that monk and say:
"The attendant who was designated by you has been duly instructed by me; go to him at the proper time, and he will provide you with a robe that is allowable."
A monk who needs a robe should approach a steward and urge and remind him two or three times:

"I have need of a robe, steward. If, while urging and reminding him two or three times, he succeeds in obtaining a robe, that is well. If he does not succeed, he may go at most four, five, or six times to stand silently in his presence.
One should remain silent while standing in the designated place; if the robe is obtained, that is well.
If it is not obtained, one should exert effort beyond that to obtain the robe.
Once the robe has been obtained, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyantikā).

If it should not be obtained, that monk must either go there in person or send a messenger to the place from which those robe-funds were brought, saying: "Those robe-funds which you, venerable sir, sent for my sake do not serve any purpose for me; may the venerable one understand this."
Lest your own interest be lost—this is the proper course of action in that regard. 10.
11. Should any monk have a new silk rug made, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
12. Should any monk have a new rug made of pure black sheep’s wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Furthermore, when a monk has a new rug made, two parts of pure black sheep’s wool must be taken.

If a monk, out of a desire for beauty, should have a new rug made consisting of two parts of pure black sheep’s wool, a third part of white wool, and a fourth part of yellowish wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense. 13.
Furthermore, when a monk has had a new rug made, he must, if he so desires, keep it for six years.

If a monk, before the lapse of six years, should have another new rug made—whether he has disposed of the old rug or not—except by the consent of the Saṃgha or out of a desire for what is excellent, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense. 14.
When a monk is having a new sitting mat made, he must take a Sugata-span from the border of his old sitting mat for the purpose of disfiguring the new one. If a monk,

without taking a Sugata-span from the border of his old sitting mat for the purpose of disfiguring the new one, should have a new sitting mat made out of a desire for something beautiful, [he commits an offense].

[If] a monk, while traveling on a road, should obtain sheep’s wool and desire it, that monk may accept it; having accepted it, he himself must carry it for a maximum distance of three *yojanas*, provided there is no one else to carry it. This is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense. 15.
Beyond that, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense for [keeping] it. 16.
Furthermore, whichever monk should have wool from sheep washed, dyed, or carded by a nun who is not a relative, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense.
17. Furthermore, whichever monk should [handle] silver with his own hand...
If a monk should either accept or cause to be accepted [silver], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense.
18. Furthermore, if a monk should engage in various kinds of transactions involving silver, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense.
19. Furthermore, if a monk should engage in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyantikā* offense. 20.
A monk may keep an extra bowl for at most ten days; if he should keep it beyond that, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, if a monk, while possessing a bowl fit for use with less than five mends remaining, should request another new bowl out of a desire for something fine, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, venerable sirs, these ninety pātayantika dharmas come up for recitation every half-month in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. [1] Intentional lying is a pātayantika.
